Text:
To assess neurovascular status in an injured extremity, check four components:

{{c1::pulse}}

{{c1::capillary refill}}

{{c1::sensation}}

{{c1::motor function}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the check runs circulation first (pulse, capillary refill), then nerve supply (sensation), then movement (motor function).

Pitfall: sensory and motor checks require patient cooperation — they cannot be assessed in an unconscious patient.

Text:
In a neurovascular check, palpate the pulse {{c2::distal::distal or proximal}} to the point of injury:

Upper extremity → the {{c1::radial}} pulse

Lower extremity → the {{c1::posterior tibial}} and {{c1::dorsalis pedis}} pulses
Back Extra:
Cue: assess the lower-extremity pulses for rate, quality, and rhythm — fast, slow, or irregular? weak, thready, or bounding?

Pitfall: pale or cyanotic skin in a hand or foot may mean poor circulation in that extremity.

Text:
In the neurovascular exam, check hand sensation by light touch at three spots:

{{c1::the flesh near the index fingertip}}

{{c1::the thumb}}

{{c1::the little finger}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an unconscious patient cannot report light touch, so this check needs a cooperative patient.

Roster: light-touch sites — hand: index fingertip · thumb · little finger; foot: flesh of the big toe · lateral side of the foot.

Text:
In the neurovascular exam, check foot sensation by light touch at two spots:

{{c1::the flesh of the big toe}}

{{c1::the lateral side of the foot}}

A patient who senses light touch in the fingers or toes distal to a fracture most likely has {{c2::an intact nerve supply::what it indicates}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: sensation sites are skin flesh (fingertips, big toe, lateral foot); pulse sites are vessels (radial, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis) — don't blur the two lists.

Roster: light-touch sites — hand: flesh near the index fingertip · thumb · little finger; foot: flesh of the big toe · lateral side of the foot.

Text: In the capillary refill test, press the tip of the fingernail or toenail until the skin blanches (turns white). If normal color does not return within {{c1::2 seconds}} of releasing the nail, assume {{c2::circulation is impaired::conclusion}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the test is typically recommended for use in children, although it can also be used in adults.

Cue: before pressing, note and record the skin color — any pallor or cyanosis.

Text: In the motor check of an injured limb (open and close a fist; wiggle the toes and move the foot up and down), if an attempted motion produces {{c1::pain}} at the injury site, stop that part of the exam — and skip the motor test entirely when the injury involves the {{c2::hand or foot}} itself.
Back Extra:
Why: the motions are performed by the hand or foot, so testing an injured hand or foot itself would cause pain — the test is meant for injuries proximal to them.

Cue: fist = upper extremity; toes and foot up-and-down = lower extremity.

Text: When evaluating the extremities, always compare the {{c1::right side with the left side}}, looking for weakness or atrophy, and assess {{c1::equality::what property}} of grip strength.
Back Extra: Cue: ask how much the patient can move each extremity or joint — never force a painful joint to move.

Text: You are assessing a 6-year-old's splinted forearm. You press her fingernail until it blanches; after release, normal color takes about 4 seconds to return. Conclusion? {{c1::Circulation in that limb is impaired::circulation judgment}}
Back Extra:
Why: normal color must return within 2 seconds of releasing the nail — 4 seconds is delayed.

Cue: capillary refill testing is typically recommended for use in children.

Text:
Report abdominal palpation findings using four descriptors:

{{c1::firm}}

{{c1::soft}}

{{c1::tender}}

{{c1::distended}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: distended = swollen.

Cue: palpate for tenderness, rigidity, and guarding — and if the patient is awake and alert, ask about pain as you examine.

Text: Always start palpation of the abdomen in the quadrant {{c1::farthest from::farthest from or closest to}} the patient's pain.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: do not palpate obvious soft-tissue injuries, and be careful not to palpate too firmly.

Cue: the four quadrants are the LUQ, LLQ, RUQ, and RLQ.

Text: A patient reports sharp pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. In which quadrant do you begin palpating? {{c1::The left upper quadrant (LUQ)::quadrant}}
Back Extra: Why: palpation always starts in the quadrant farthest from the pain — for RLQ pain, the diagonal opposite is the LUQ.

Text: When a patient reports no pelvic pain, apply gentle pressure to the pelvis — never {{c1::rock::motion}} it.
Back Extra:
Why: rocking can worsen (exacerbate) damage to any unstable bones.

Pitfall: pelvic and surrounding abdominal injuries can bleed profusely with no obvious external signs — keep monitoring mental status, skin condition, and vital signs.

Cue: any movement, crepitus, or reported pain or tenderness on gentle pressure = possible severe injury.

Text: Pulse oximetry evaluates the effectiveness of {{c1::oxygenation::oxygenation or ventilation}}. The pulse oximeter is a {{c1::photoelectric::device type}} device that monitors the {{c1::oxygen saturation of hemoglobin}} in the capillary beds.
Back Extra:
Meaning: hemoglobin = the iron-containing part of the red blood cell that oxygen attaches to.

Pitfall: a monitoring device is an adjunct — it never replaces your comprehensive assessment of the patient.

Cue: normal ambient-air values mostly fall between 94% and 99%, varying with altitude.

Text: Because the pulse oximeter's light source must have unobstructed access to a capillary bed, {{c1::dark fingernail polish}} might need to be removed before clipping on the probe.
Back Extra:
Why: the sensing probe clips onto a finger or earlobe and shines light through the capillary bed — anything opaque over the nail corrupts the reading.

Cue: results appear as a percentage on the display screen.

Text: A pulse oximeter functions properly only with adequate {{c1::perfusion}} and adequate numbers of {{c1::red blood cells::blood component}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the sensor reads blood in a capillary bed — vasoconstriction empties the bed, and lost red cells leave less hemoglobin to read.

Pitfall: never let a good-looking SpO2 number prevent oxygen for a patient who reports difficulty breathing.

Text: A pulse oximeter presumes {{c1::oxygen}} is what saturates the hemoglobin, so any chemical that {{c1::displaces oxygen}} — such as {{c1::carbon monoxide::toxic gas}} — may cause misleading values.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the pulse oximeter is only a tool — not a substitute for a good assessment.

Distinguish: low-perfusion states (vasoconstriction, blood loss) break the reading differently — too little capillary blood to read, versus the wrong chemical riding the hemoglobin.

Text: During a winter power outage, two adults are found barely responsive in a home where a charcoal grill has been burning indoors. The monitor shows SpO2 98%, but the reading cannot be trusted because inhaled {{c1::carbon monoxide::gas}} may have {{c1::displaced the oxygen}} on their hemoglobin.
Back Extra: Cue: the oximeter only presumes oxygen is what saturates hemoglobin — it cannot tell which chemical is actually aboard.

Text: A patient in shock has pale, cool skin. The monitor shows SpO2 99%. That value may be {{c1::inaccurate or misleading::trust judgment}}.
Back Extra:
Why: shock causes vasoconstriction, and the pulse oximeter needs an adequately perfused capillary bed (and enough red blood cells) to read accurately.

Pitfall: bleeding and anemia break the reading the same way — too few red blood cells to read.

Text: {{c1::Capnography::monitoring method}} is a {{c2::noninvasive}} method that quickly and efficiently provides information on a patient's {{c2::ventilation}}, {{c2::circulation}}, and {{c2::metabolism}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: oxygen burns the fuel of metabolism and carbon dioxide is the exhaust — capnography measures that exhaust in exhaled air.

Distinguish: pulse oximetry shows how much oxygen is available to the cells; measuring exhaled CO2 shows how much is being used.

Cue: monitors attach to the end of an advanced airway or onto a nasal cannula.

Text: Waveform capnography shows a graph of how {{c1::easily}}, how {{c1::frequently}}, and how {{c1::much}} the patient is exhaling carbon dioxide.
Back Extra: Cue: capnography is used to evaluate breathing treatments and artificial ventilation and to confirm endotracheal tube placement; it correlates with lactic acid values in septic shock.

Text:
Check a blood glucose level in three patient groups:

all patients {{c1::known to have diabetes}}

all patients with {{c1::an altered mental status}}

patients with {{c1::generalized malaise or weakness}}
Back Extra:
Cue: in addition, a blood glucose level can be assessed in any patient you think has a poor general impression.

Why: a low level can explain why a patient is unresponsive; a high level with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and a mental-status change may signal dangerous complications of high blood glucose.

Text: A 58-year-old has no specific complaint — he just feels weak all over. What bedside level should you assess? {{c1::Blood glucose}}
Back Extra: Why: generalized malaise or weakness is one of the three standing indications for glucometry, alongside known diabetes and altered mental status.

Text: When reassessing vital signs, compare the baseline set — obtained during the {{c1::primary assessment::assessment phase}} — with any and all subsequent vital signs, and look for trends.
Back Extra:
Cue: the trend questions — have the vitals increased, declined, or stayed the same? If so, how fast?

Why: reassessment exists to identify and treat changes in the patient's condition — also recheck mental status, airway, breathing, circulation, and skin color and temperature.
